9.after: or property that departs — māl rāyiḥ
9.note: Niasse gives both readings. Al-Bukhārī (no. 4555) has rāyiḥ, which the printing's own note follows; Muslim (no. 1664) has rābiḥ. Whether the disjunctive is Niasse's or the transcriber's cannot be settled from the copy-text.

9.after: So he handed it over to Usāma, his son.
9.note: A clause of four words stands here which the copy-text has garbled past recovery. Its sense bears on whether the verse was still being recited when Zayd made his gift.

9.after: It was named Bakka because it breaks the necks of tyrants.
9.note: Bakka as a dialectal variant of Makka; the derivation from bakka, to crush, is the one Niasse prefers.

9.after: Al-Jalāl said: ⟨and between the two was forty years⟩, and this is a slip of the pen on his part.
9.note: Niasse corrects al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī. The forty years belong to the interval between the two buildings of Ādam, not between the Kaʿba and al-Aqṣā.

9.after: it is as though he has clasped the hand of the Lord, Blessed and Exalted⟩
9.note: The report as Niasse gives it. The printing's apparatus cites it in the wording al-ḥajar yamīn Allāh fī al-arḍ yuṣāfiḥu bihā ʿibādahu (al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, no. 3804); his wording is translated as he gives it.

9.after: he is nearer to two than he is to three, and nearer to one than to two.⟩
9.note: Niasse's wording departs from the Tirmidhī text cited in the printing's apparatus.

9.after: the Watcher is all-seeing — sincerity is needed.
9.note: Ṣirr at Q. 3:117 is rendered neutrally. Niasse glosses it ḥarr aw bard shadīd, intense heat or cold, against the usual gloss of intense cold alone, and the English keeps his wider reading.

9.after: on the Saturday, the seventh of Shawwāl, in the third year of the Hijra
9.note: As Niasse gives the date. The reports more often place Uḥud on the fifteenth of Shawwāl.

9.after: «Will it not suffice you that your Lord
9.note: Niasse apportions the five thousand as Jibrīl two thousand, Mīkāʾīl one thousand, Isrāfīl one thousand and the Angel of Death one thousand. The report in the printing's apparatus gives Jibrīl two thousand, Mīkāʾīl two thousand and Isrāfīl one thousand, with no mention of the Angel of Death.

9.after: You will not find the word ‘victory
9.note: The ḥadīth of Uḥud is given here as kayfa yufliḥu qawmun khaḍabū wajha nabiyyihim bi-l-dam. Muslim and al-Bukhārī have shajjū nabiyyahum wa-kasarū rubāʿiyyatahu.

9.after: He forgives whom He will» — him for whom He wills forgiveness
9.note: The ḥadīth of the whip is given in an expanded wording. Al-Bukhārī (no. 3250) has mawḍiʿu sawṭin fī al-janna khayrun min al-dunyā wa-mā fīhā.

9.after: until, when He seizes him, He does not let him go.⟩
9.note: The clause hādhā waʿd min Allāh … waffāhu man qablanā will not construe as pointed: man qablanā is marked as subject where the sense requires an indirect object.

9.after: Iblīs the accursed cried out and said: Muhammad has been killed!
9.note: The copy-text has lanā ʿUzzā wa-lā ʿUzzā lakum for the received lanā al-ʿUzzā wa-lā ʿUzzā lakum, and is translated as it stands.

9.after: ⟨al-Jalīl has sworn that He will not punish a servant whose name is Muhammad or Aḥmad.⟩
9.note: The saying is not identified. The printing's apparatus at this point cites a different report, from ʿIyāḍ, al-Shifāʾ 1:176.

9.after: that there be in his house a Muhammad, and two Muhammads, and three.⟩
9.note: The printing leaves the quotation unclosed. It is closed here on the authority of the apparatus (al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr 2:499), whose wording — mā ḍarra aḥadakum law kāna — differs from Niasse's and is not substituted for it.

9.after: «nor did they submit» — they did not yield to their enemy on account of the death of their prophet
9.note: Q. 3:146 is taken as qutila, passive, with the copy-text and with Niasse's own gloss: if Muhammad is killed, many prophets before him were killed. The reading qātala is not followed.

9.after: «and Allah loves the steadfast» (Q. 3:146) — He rewards them.
9.note: Four tokens follow the gloss al-janna in the copy-text which yield no sense.

9.after: at Uḥud; and they were the Muslims, all but twelve men
9.note: The count is Niasse's. The reports usually name a smaller number who held firm.

9.after: «Indeed Allah loves those who rely» (Q. 3:159) — upon Him.
9.note: The ḥadīth of the seventy thousand is given in a wording that differs from al-Bukhārī and Muslim, who have lā yastarqūna wa-lā yaktawūna wa-lā yataṭayyarūna wa-ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn.

9.after: that range through the Garden wherever they wish, as comes in the hadith
9.note: Niasse attributes the report to ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd, as Muslim does; elsewhere it is given from Jābir.
